attempts.final_doc:
# Change Plan — Adding a Field to the `billing-events` Stream

**Prepared for:** the owner of the `billing-events` stream
**Date prepared:** 2026-08-09
**Status:** executable as written, subject to the open items in §14
**Basis:** the platform knowledge pages listed in §15. Everything asserted below is drawn from those pages; where they are silent, this plan says so rather than filling the gap.

---

## 1. Scope of this plan

This plan covers adding one new field to the records carried by `billing-events`, from first proposal to the field being live and documented.

**The field itself is not specified by the platform's recorded material.** Nothing in the catalog or the knowledge pages describes a pending or proposed field for this stream — the catalog returned no `billing-events` entity at all, and the only field-level record is the *Billing Events Field Guide*, which describes the fields that exist today. This plan is therefore written to be field-agnostic: every step applies whatever the field turns out to be, and the points where the field's specifics change the path (compatibility, population rules, egress) are called out explicitly at those points.

The field's name, type, which of the five states populate it, and whether it carries personal or regulated content must be filled in by the owner before §5 can be executed.

---

## 2. Classification — read this before planning anything else

This is the single decision that governs the whole plan, and it is the one most likely to be got wrong.

`billing-events` is a **regulated-tier** stream (*Billing Events Stream Runbook*). A stream enters that tier when a downstream consumer is obliged to reproduce its contents on demand; the tier is assigned by the data governance group and reviewed annually (*Regulated Tier Operating Rules*).

**Every regulated-tier stream is governed by change class CC-3** (*Regulated Tier Operating Rules*). This is a property of the stream, not of the change. It is stated without exception for additive changes.

### The trap

The natural reading of *Change Class Reference* is that adding a field is "CC-2 — additive: a compatible addition to a published interface. The owning team signs it off and consumers are given two business days of advance notice." **That reading is wrong for this stream.** The regulated-tier rule assigns the class at the stream level and overrides the per-change reading. Planning this change as CC-2 would understate the notice by seven business days and would take the sign-off from the wrong body.

### What CC-3 means, concretely

| | CC-3 (what applies) | CC-2 (what does *not* apply) |
|---|---|---|
| Sign-off | The governance group | The owning team |
| Advance notice to consumers | **9 business days** | 2 business days |

Also from *Regulated Tier Operating Rules*: **a change the stream owner believes needs less notice than its class requires is not a shortcut the owner can take — it is a request to reclassify the stream, and it is handled by the governance group.** If nine business days is genuinely unworkable, the route is a reclassification request, not a faster change. The material does not record how long a reclassification request takes or what evidence it needs.

The only route that applies a change ahead of its notice is **CC-5 — emergency**, covered in §12. It is not available for a planned field addition.

---

## 3. Approvals required

Every approval below is a distinct gate. None is implied by another.

| # | Approval | Whose | Recorded source | When |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | **CC-3 sign-off on the change** | The data governance group | *Change Class Reference*, *Regulated Tier Operating Rules* | Before the announcement goes out (the announcement must name who signed it off) |
| A2 | **Schema version acceptance** | The schema registry, mechanically — it refuses a version incompatible with the stream's declared compatibility mode | *Schema Registry Operations* | Before any producer writes the new version |
| A3 | **Producer attestation, per producing service** | The named owner of each of the three producing services | *Regulated Tier Operating Rules* | After the change ("at onboarding and after any change") — see §10 |
| A4 | **Egress approval** — *only if* the new field flows to a destination the platform does not operate | The data governance group | *Data Egress Approval Policy* | Before the field reaches that destination |
| A5 | **Reclassification** — *only if* the owner seeks less than 9 business days' notice | The data governance group | *Regulated Tier Operating Rules* | Instead of, not alongside, a shortened notice |

Note that A1 and A4 both sit with the governance group but are separate decisions. An approved egress additionally needs a named recipient, a stated purpose, and an end date; a route without an end date is not approved, and a route whose end date passes is disabled automatically rather than reviewed.

**Gap:** the material does not record who sits in the data governance group, how a CC-3 proposal is submitted to it, what form the proposal takes, how often it meets, or how long it takes to return a decision. The notice clock only starts at announcement, and announcement requires sign-off already in hand — so the governance turnaround is dead time ahead of the nine days, of unknown length. Budget for it and confirm the lead time with the group before committing to a date.

---

## 4. Timing constraints

Four separate rules constrain when this change may be applied. All four bind simultaneously.

### 4.1 The nine-business-day notice

From *Change Class Reference*: notice is counted **in business days from the announcement to the change window opening, excluding the announcement day itself.** So the announcement day is day zero and nine full business days must pass before the window may open.

### 4.2 The ledger close freeze

From *Ledger Close Calendar*: **platform changes that touch anything the ledger reads are frozen from the last working day of the month to the second working day of the next.**

This freeze applies to this change. The chain is recorded: `billing-events` feeds every finance-facing report "directly or through the settled-invoice view" (*Billing Events Stream Runbook*), and the nightly `ledger-reconcile` job compares the settled-invoice view against the general ledger extract (*Ledger Reconcile Job Runbook*). The stream is upstream of what the ledger reads.

The freeze does not stop an incident response, and a change applied during a freeze for incident reasons is recorded as such — that is the CC-5 path in §12, not a planned-change path.

### 4.3 Interaction of the two

From *Change Class Reference*: **a notice period that would end inside a change freeze runs to the first business day after the freeze lifts.** The notice does not expire during the freeze and the window does not open the moment the freeze ends mid-notice — the notice is extended to that first business day after the lift.

### 4.4 Records inside a closed period are never restated

From *Ledger Close Calendar*: records dated inside a closed period are never restated in place; a correction is posted into the open period with a reference back. This forecloses any plan that would retroactively populate the new field onto already-closed billing records. See §9.3.

### 4.5 Worked calendar (illustrative)

Assuming an announcement on **Monday 2026-08-10**, and assuming no public holidays (see the gap below):

| Business day | Date |
|---|---|
| Announcement (day 0, excluded) | Mon 2026-08-10 |
| 1–4 | Tue 08-11 → Fri 08-14 |
| 5–9 | Mon 08-17 → Fri 08-21 |
| **Earliest the change window may open** | **Mon 2026-08-24** |
| August freeze (last working day of Aug → second working day of Sep) | Mon 08-31 → Wed 09-02 |

A window on 2026-08-24 through 2026-08-28 sits clear of the freeze. A window slipping to 08-31 or later is blocked until **Thu 2026-09-03**.

If instead the announcement slipped such that day 9 fell on 08-31, 09-01 or 09-02, the notice would run to Thu 2026-09-03 under §4.3.

**Gap:** the material defines notice in "business days" and the freeze in "working days" but records no holiday calendar and no definition of either term. Confirm both against the organisation's calendar before fixing dates; a single holiday inside the window moves the earliest opening by a day.

### 4.6 Time of day

The material sets **no** time-of-day rule for applying a stream change. For information, the overnight schedule is fully allocated (*Nightly Batch Window Calendar*): collector drain 22:00–23:15, raw exports 23:15–00:45, maintenance and vacuum 00:45–02:00, aggregation 02:00–04:00, reconciliation 04:00–05:30. The general ledger extract is due nightly at 03:40, and by 06:00 on the first two working days of a month. Choosing an hour outside 22:00–05:30 keeps the change clear of the reconciliation that reads downstream of this stream, but this is a recommendation from the surrounding material, not a recorded rule.

---

## 5. Phase 0 — Discovery, before the proposal is written

Nothing here needs an approval, and all of it is needed to write the proposal.

1. **Read the current field set.** *Billing Events Field Guide* is the recorded home of field meaning. It records: the state field takes one of five values (created, activated, moved, settled, refunded) and states are **not ordered** — a subscription may move several times between activation and settlement, and a refund may follow a settlement by months. Two money fields travel on each record, both integers in minor units, both in the account's own currency, with no converted amount on the record. The reason code and the original reference are populated **only** on refunded records.

2. **Decide the new field's population rule against the state enumeration.** Say explicitly, in the proposal, which of the five states populate the field and which leave it absent. The field guide records exactly why this matters: treating an absent reason code as "no reason given" misreports every non-refund record as a refund without a reason. A new field with a state-dependent population rule and no documented rule reproduces that defect.

3. **Decide units and currency if the field is a money field.** The recorded convention is integer minor units in the account's own currency, with conversion left to reporting against the rate table for the settlement date. A new money field that departs from this convention needs to say so loudly; one that follows it needs to say that too.

4. **Pull the consumer list from the consumer contract registry.** The registry records, per consumer: the consuming service, the schema version it reads, an owner who can be reached, and whether the consumer is idempotent (*Consumer Contract Registry*). This list is what the announcement is sent to.

5. **Pull the producer list.** *Billing Events Stream Runbook* records that three services produce to the stream. Each producing service names an owner (*Regulated Tier Operating Rules*, *Stream Onboarding Checklist*). All three must be identified now, because all three attest at §10.

6. **Look up the stream's declared compatibility mode in the schema registry.** This determines whether §7 runs its compatible branch or its staged branch. **Gap:** the declared compatibility mode for `billing-events` is not recorded in any knowledge page. It must be read from the registry itself; do not assume that adding a field is compatible under it.

7. **Check the registry for stale contracts.** A contract not confirmed for a year is flagged in the quarterly review as a probable orphan; flagged contracts are confirmed or removed, never left flagged (*Consumer Contract Registry*). Resolve flagged contracts before announcing, or the announcement goes to owners who are no longer there.

**Gaps at this phase:**
- The identities of the three producing services, their owners, the current schema version, and the registered consumer list are not recorded in the platform's knowledge pages. They exist in the contract registry and the schema registry; read them from there.
- The *Stream Onboarding Checklist* explicitly states that it "covers putting a producer on a stream. It does not cover changing what the stream carries." Do not use it as the checklist for this change.
- The platform holds no change-proposal template or reference document (searched across resources, assets, context documents and prompts; none exist). The proposal structure in §6 is assembled from the requirements the various pages impose, not from a recorded template.

---

## 6. Phase 1 — Proposal and governance sign-off

**Approval gate: A1.**

Submit to the data governance group a proposal containing, at minimum, everything the later steps will need to be true:

- The field: name, type, and meaning.
- Which of the five states populate it, and what its absence means on the states that do not.
- Units and currency, if it is a money field.
- Whether it carries content that would make any existing route an egress under *Data Egress Approval Policy* — i.e. whether it would be written to a destination the platform does not operate. If so, an egress request (A4) with named recipient, stated purpose and end date goes alongside this proposal.
- The stream's declared compatibility mode and whether the addition is compatible under it, i.e. which branch of §7 applies.
- The consumer list from the registry and, for each, the schema version pinned and whether the consumer is idempotent.
- The proposed change window, dated against §4.
- The rollback position (§11).

Do **not** proceed to §8 until sign-off is in hand and you can name who signed it — the announcement is required to carry that name.

**Gap:** the material records that the governance group signs CC-3 changes off, but records nothing about the submission channel, the required proposal format, or the decision turnaround.

---

## 7. Phase 2 — Register or stage the schema version

**Approval gate: A2.** From *Schema Registry Operations*: a schema version is registered **before** a producer writes it, and the registry refuses a version incompatible with the stream's declared compatibility mode.

The staging mechanics say nothing about *when* the change may happen — that remains the change class's business (§4). Registering a version is not applying the change.

### 7.1 If the new version is compatible under the declared mode

Register the new version. The registry accepts it. Producers may write it only once the change window has opened (§9).

### 7.2 If the new version is incompatible under the declared mode

The version is **staged, not registered**:

1. Write the new version to a shadow subject.
2. Move consumers across **one at a time**.
3. Promote the subject once the last consumer reads the new version cleanly.

This branch changes the shape of the whole plan: the cutover is no longer a single window action but a per-consumer migration, and "the field is live" means "the subject has been promoted after the last consumer read it cleanly." Consumers that move in this branch are each changing the version they read, which re-triggers contract confirmation (§10.2).

Note also that a change which *invalidates a published contract* is CC-4, not CC-3 — a full quarter of notice, and the old contract runs in parallel until the last consumer has moved (*Change Class Reference*). **If the compatibility check reveals that the addition invalidates a published contract, stop and re-classify with the governance group before announcing.** The nine-day plan does not apply to a CC-4 change.

---

## 8. Phase 3 — The announcement

From *Change Announcement Channels*, an announcement goes to **three places at once**:

1. The platform mailing list.
2. The platform channel.
3. **The registry entry for the interface being changed — this is the authoritative one,** because it is the only channel a consumer onboarded after the announcement will still see.

Who the mailing reaches is decided by the contracts registered against the interface. **A consumer that never registered is not announced to** — this is why registration is a condition of read access rather than a courtesy. Do not construct a side-list of consumers you happen to know about; the registry is the list.

The announcement must contain exactly four things:

- **What is changing.**
- **The window it will be applied in.**
- **Who signed it off** (from A1).
- **How a consumer says it is not ready.**

And it must **not** contain a justification. The recorded reason: consumers act on the change, not on the reason for it.

The announcement day is day zero of the nine (§4.1).

**Gap:** the announcement is required to tell consumers how to say they are not ready, but the material does not record what happens when one does — whether a not-ready response defers the window, whether it is a veto, who arbitrates, or what the deadline for raising it is. This must be settled with the governance group at A1 and stated concretely in the announcement, because an announcement cannot satisfy its own content requirement without it.

---

## 9. Phase 4 — The notice period, and applying the change

### 9.1 During the nine days

- Consumers assess against the announcement and respond via the mechanism the announcement names.
- Consumers that intend to move to the new version prepare to do so; each such move re-triggers contract confirmation (§10.2).
- Nothing is written in the new version yet.

### 9.2 In the window

1. Confirm the window still sits clear of the ledger close freeze (§4.2) — re-check, because a slipped window can drift into a freeze that the original date cleared.
2. Producers begin writing the registered version (compatible branch), or the shadow subject is promoted after the last consumer reads cleanly (staged branch).
3. The field is live.

### 9.3 Records written before the cutover

The stream retains **fourteen days** of records and can be replayed from any offset inside that window (*Billing Events Stream Runbook*; the retention floor of fourteen days is a regulated-tier obligation, *Regulated Tier Operating Rules*). Records written before the cutover do not carry the new field. For at least fourteen days after the change, any replay that crosses the cutover offset delivers a mix of records with and without it.

Consumers need to be told that, in the field's documentation, in the same terms the *Billing Events Field Guide* already uses for the refund-only fields: **absence before the cutover means "not yet written", not a value.**

**Gap:** the material does not record whether backfilling a new field into already-retained records is permitted, or by what mechanism. What it does record cuts against retroactive restatement of billing history: a replay "is not a repair — a record that was never written cannot be replayed" (*Billing Events Replay Guide*), and records dated inside a closed ledger period are never restated in place (*Ledger Close Calendar*). Treat backfill as a separate question for the governance group, not as part of this change.

If a replay is performed for any reason around the cutover, the replay rules apply in full: choose the offset **by timestamp, not by count** (counting back is wrong whenever a producer has been backfilling); **pause the consumers that are not idempotent** — the contract registry says which ones those are, and a paused consumer resumes from its own committed offset so nothing is lost; and **confirm afterwards** by comparing the record count in the replayed window against the count the consumer processed.

---

## 10. Phase 5 — After the change

### 10.1 Producer attestation (A3)

Each producing service's named owner attests, **after any change**, that the records it writes are complete (*Regulated Tier Operating Rules*). All three producers attest. This is a regulated-tier obligation and is not discharged by the change having been signed off.

### 10.2 Consumer contract re-confirmation

**Contracts are re-confirmed when a consumer changes the version it reads** (*Consumer Contract Registry*). Every consumer that moves onto the new version re-confirms its contract, recording the new version, its owner, and whether it is idempotent. In the staged branch this happens per consumer as each is moved across; in the compatible branch it happens as consumers choose to move.

Consumers that stay on their pinned version do not re-confirm on account of this change. Note that a registered version is never deleted, only superseded, so a consumer that pinned a version still resolves it (*Schema Registry Operations*).

### 10.3 Documentation

The *Billing Events Field Guide* is the recorded home of field-by-field meaning for this stream. Update it with the new field: its meaning, which states populate it, what its absence means, and — if it is a money field — its units and currency. This is a recommendation drawn from where the material keeps this information; the pages do not record a rule obliging a documentation update after a schema change.

The announcement's registry entry remains the authoritative record for consumers onboarded after the change (§8), so it must survive as an accurate description of what changed, not be superseded by the field guide.

### 10.4 Standing obligations unchanged by this change

Neither of these is triggered by the change, but both continue and neither is waived by it:

- Every principal with read access is re-confirmed each quarter; an unconfirmed principal loses access **at the review date**, not after a grace period.
- The regulated-tier assignment is reviewed annually by the governance group.

---

## 11. Rollback

From *Schema Registry Operations*: **a registered version is never deleted, only superseded.** Rolling back means registering the previous definition as a new version, so the history reads forward and a consumer that pinned a version still resolves it.

Practically:

- To withdraw the field, register the pre-change definition as a **new, later** version. Do not attempt to delete or rewrite the version that introduced the field.
- Records already written with the field keep it. The stream's fourteen-day window will contain records carrying a field that the current version does not define.
- In the staged branch, a rollback before promotion means simply not promoting the shadow subject and moving any migrated consumers back — the recorded mechanic is consumer-at-a-time in both directions.

**Gap:** the material does not record whether a rollback is itself a change requiring its own class, notice and sign-off. Two readings are available and they differ by nine business days. Settle this with the governance group at A1 and write the answer into the proposal, so that the rollback position is pre-approved rather than argued during an incident. Absent that, the safe assumption is that a rollback carried out because the change caused a defect runs the CC-5 route in §12.

---

## 12. If the change has to happen (or be undone) out of course — CC-5

**CC-5 — emergency** is a change applied ahead of its notice because leaving the defect in place is worse (*Change Class Reference*). It is:

- **Signed off by the duty manager**, not by the governance group.
- Applied first; **the notice is reconstructed afterwards, with the reason recorded.**

The duty manager role rotates monthly among the platform leads and is published a quarter ahead (*Duty Manager Rota*). A duty manager who will be unreachable names a standing delegate who **holds** the role rather than assisting in it — there is never a state in which two people hold it or nobody does. So there is always exactly one person who can sign a CC-5, and the rota says who. The duty manager's primary channel is phone, fallback pager app (*Paging Channel Directory*).

The ledger close freeze does not stop an incident response, and a change applied during a freeze for incident reasons is recorded as such (*Ledger Close Calendar*).

CC-5 is not a route around the nine days for a planned field addition. It exists for the case where this change, once live, turns out to be the defect.

---

## 13. If the change breaks something

Anyone may open an incident, and the bias toward opening one is deliberate: opening one costs almost nothing, not opening one costs the timeline (*Opening and Closing an Incident*). An incident needs, at the start, only a one-line statement of what is wrong, the system it is wrong in, and who opened it.

### Banding (*Incident Severity Bands*)

The band is a statement about consequence, not effort — a small defect with an accounting consequence outranks a large one without.

- **Band A** — the change has already produced an incorrect external figure, or customer-visible loss of service. Notified immediately to the whole platform group. **Red route.**
- **Band B** — an internal control has stopped proving what it exists to prove, with no external figure yet affected. Notified to the owning team and the platform group's shift lead. **Amber route.** This is the band the most likely failure mode lands in: `ledger-reconcile` **failures on three consecutive nights open a band B incident**, because at that point the reconciliation has not been proved for a full accounting period (*Ledger Reconcile Job Runbook*). If the change is going to break the reconcile, this is the clock it breaks it on.
- **Band C** — degradation with a known workaround already in place. Standard route.
- **Band D** — no consequence before the next working day. Standard route.

Distinguish a *break* from a *failure*: a break is one discrepancy written by the reconciliation, not a failure of the reconciliation itself; a job fails when it cannot complete, and reports a problem when it completes and does not like what it saw (*Platform Glossary*). A schema change is far more likely to produce breaks than failures, and the two are worked by different people on different clocks.

### Escalation (*Escalation Ladders*, *Duty Manager Response Matrix*)

| Route | Rungs | Clocks (max time on each rung before it climbs) |
|---|---|---|
| Red (band A) | shift lead → duty manager → head of platform → executive on call | 5 min → 10 min → 30 min |
| Amber (band B) | shift lead → duty manager → head of platform | 20 min → 25 min → 2 hours |
| Standard (bands C, D) | shift lead → owning team's manager (working hours only) | 4 hours → next working day |

An incident starts at the first rung and climbs one at a time; skipping a rung is allowed only when the person on it is the one escalating. The clock starts when the incident is **opened**, not when it is acknowledged, and runs across shift handovers; an unacknowledged expired clock climbs on its own. Every climb writes a line to the record. Between 22:00 and 06:00 the standard route's clocks are doubled; **red and amber are worked to the same clocks at every hour.**

### While it is open (*Incident Communication Guide*)

The opening notice says what is affected, what is not, and when the next update will come — not the cause. Updates go out on the promised cadence, **including the ones that say nothing has changed**, because a silent incident reads as a resolved one. Only the incident lead speaks to anyone outside the platform group. Avoid "should be fixed", "briefly", "minor"; say what was observed and what was done.

### Closing and the record

Closing needs evidence the condition has gone, not an absence of further reports; for a scheduled job that means a **clean scheduled run** — a manual run does not clear an open incident (*Opening and Closing an Incident*, *Ledger Reconcile Job Runbook*). Every closed incident leaves a record with four parts: timeline (including the observations that turned out to be irrelevant), contributing conditions (written as conditions, not causes), corrections (each with an owner — a correction with no owner is a wish), and review by someone who was not involved (*Incident Postmortem Standard*). An incident is never deleted; one opened by mistake is closed as such.

---

# Incident Handling Document — `ledger-reconcile` Failed on Three Consecutive Nights

**Applies to:** the nightly `ledger-reconcile` job, after its third consecutive failed scheduled run.
**Audience:** the on-shift engineer who discovers or is handed the third failure.
**Document date:** 2026-08-09.

---

## 1. Scope and trigger

The `ledger-reconcile` job compares the settled-invoice view against the general ledger extract and writes one row per discrepancy. Each discrepancy is a **break**. Breaks are normal in small numbers and are worked the next morning through break triage — they are not what this document covers.

This document covers the job **failing**: the job could not complete. The platform glossary draws this line deliberately — a job *fails* when it cannot complete, and *reports a problem* when it completes and does not like what it saw. The two are worked by different people on different clocks, and conflating them is the stated reason most overnight pages reach the wrong person. If the job completed and merely wrote a large number of breaks, stop here and use the Reconcile Break Triage Guide instead.

**The trigger is explicit:** a single failure is retried automatically on the next schedule and opens nothing. **Failures on three consecutive nights open a severity band B incident.** The reasoning recorded in the runbook is that at that point the reconciliation has not been proved for a full accounting period, and the question is no longer whether the job runs.

The job runs in the 04:00–05:30 reconciliation window. Its input, the general ledger extract, is due nightly at 03:40, and by 06:00 on the first two working days of a month when the close batch runs ahead of it.

---

## 2. Before you open: confirm the trigger actually fired

Confirm all three of the following. Do not spend long on this — opening an incident costs almost nothing and not opening one costs the timeline, so the recorded bias is toward opening.

1. **Three failures, on three consecutive nights, of the scheduled run.** The Overnight Failure Review exists precisely to notice this: it reads three nights at a time, because a job that failed once is noise and the same job failing on consecutive nights is the thing the review exists to catch.
2. **They are failures, not break reports.** See §1.
3. **The current night's run log says so.** The Reconcile Failure History page ends with an explicit warning that nothing in it is a substitute for the current night's run log. Use the history for pattern recognition only.

> **Where the material is silent:** nothing available states whether a *successful manual* run on one of the three nights breaks the consecutive streak. The runbook does say a manual run "does not settle whether the scheduled job is healthy," and that the incident closes on the scheduled run rather than a manual one. Read the count as three consecutive failed *scheduled* runs, and record in the incident that you made that reading.

---

## 3. Open the incident

**Who may open it:** anyone. You do not need permission and you do not need a complete picture. An incident that waits for a complete picture before it exists has no early timeline, which is the part that is hardest to reconstruct later.

**Severity band: B.** Assigned at the moment of opening. Band B is defined as *an internal control that has stopped proving what it exists to prove, with no external figure yet affected* — which is exactly this situation, and matches the runbook's own instruction that three consecutive failures open a band B incident.

**Fill in at the start — these three fields only:**

| Field | Value for this incident |
| --- | --- |
| One-line statement of what is wrong | e.g. "`ledger-reconcile` has failed on three consecutive scheduled runs; the reconciliation is unproved for those business dates." |
| The system it is wrong in | The nightly `ledger-reconcile` job (reconciliation window, 04:00–05:30). |
| Who opened it | You, by name. |

Everything else is filled in as it is learned. Record the **open timestamp precisely** — every escalation clock in §5 is measured from it.

**Re-band upward immediately if either becomes true:**
- An incorrect external figure has already been produced, or there is customer-visible loss of service → **band A**, red route, notified immediately to the whole platform group.

Do not band down. Band C ("a degradation with a known workaround already in place") does not apply: a manual run is explicitly not a workaround that settles the job's health. Band D ("no consequence before the next working day") does not apply, because the consequence — an unproved control across an accounting period — is already present.

**The band is a statement about consequence, not about effort.** A small defect with an accounting consequence outranks a large one without.

> **Where the material is silent:** no incident tracking system, ticket prefix, or form is named anywhere in the available material. Open the incident in whatever record your team uses, and note in it that the tool was not specified by the handbook.

---

## 4. Who has to be told

Band B is notified to:

1. **The owning team** of `ledger-reconcile`.
2. **The platform group's shift lead.**

Send this notification at the moment you open, before you begin diagnosis. The first-rung escalation clock is already running (§5).

> **Where the material is silent:** the available material never names the owning team for `ledger-reconcile`, nor names any individual. It refers throughout to roles — "the owning team's shift lead," "the platform duty manager," "the head of platform." Resolve the current holders from the on-call roster and the duty manager rota, which are the sources of truth:
> - **Shift lead / on-call:** week-long shifts, handed over Tuesday mornings so a weekend never falls across a handover. Swaps are arranged directly between engineers and recorded in the roster *before* the shift starts. **The roster is the source of truth, not the conversation that preceded it** — an unrecorded swap is the single most common reason a page reaches the wrong person.
> - **Duty manager:** rotates monthly among the platform leads, published a quarter ahead. If the holder named a standing delegate for this window, **the delegate holds the role**, not assists in it — there is never a state where two people hold it or nobody does. A rota corrected less than a day ahead is announced in the platform channel as well as recorded, so check the channel if the rota looks stale.

Note that the **batch review shift** — the engineer who reads the overnight run logs each morning and who most likely surfaced the third failure — is a daytime duty and **carries no pager**. Do not treat that engineer as a rung or as reachable out of hours. The review is a reading, not a repair: anything needing fixing is handed to the owning team with what the review found.

---

## 5. Escalation

### 5.1 The route

Band B follows the **amber route**. An incident occupies exactly one rung at a time and climbs one rung at a time. Skipping a rung is allowed only when the person on that rung is the one escalating.

| Rung | Who |
| --- | --- |
| First | The owning team's shift lead |
| Second | The platform duty manager |
| Third | The head of platform |

The amber route ends at the third rung. (The red route continues to a fourth rung, the executive on call; amber does not.)

### 5.2 The clocks

Each figure below is the longest the incident may sit on that rung before it **must reach the next one**.

| Rung | Amber clock | Must have reached the next rung by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First — shift lead | 20 minutes | T+20 min from open |
| Second — duty manager | 25 minutes | T+45 min from open |
| Third — head of platform | 2 hours | See the note below |

Rules that govern these clocks, all stated explicitly in the response matrix:

- **The clock starts when the incident is opened, not when it is acknowledged.** Waiting for someone to answer does not pause anything.
- **It runs across shift handovers.** A handover does not reset it.
- **An unacknowledged clock that expires climbs on its own.** The escalation is automatic. The acknowledgement, when it eventually comes, is recorded late — the escalation is *not* held back for it.
- **The amber route is worked to the same clocks at every hour.** The overnight doubling between 22:00 and 06:00 applies **only to the standard route**, because the rung below it is on a pager rather than at a desk. The matrix states the reason plainly: an incident on the red or amber route is already past the point where the hour is an excuse. Since `ledger-reconcile` runs 04:00–05:30, this incident will normally be opened inside those hours — **you do not get doubled clocks, and you do not wait for morning.**

> **Where the material is silent, and it matters here:** the matrix gives the amber route a third-rung figure of 2 hours, but the amber route has no fourth rung. What the incident is required to do when the head of platform's 2-hour clock expires is not specified anywhere available. Treat the 2-hour mark as a hard checkpoint: at T+2h45 from open, if the incident is still unacknowledged at the third rung, record the expiry in the incident record as an expired clock with no defined destination, and raise it with the duty manager (or their delegate) as an unresolved gap in the ladder. Do not invent a fourth rung.
>
> A second, smaller ambiguity: the matrix fixes the anchor only for the first clock ("starts when the incident is opened"). The cumulative times in the table above read the second and third figures as starting when the incident reaches those rungs. Record which reading you used.

### 5.3 How each rung is actually reached

| Role | Primary channel | Fallback |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shift lead | Pager app | Phone |
| Duty manager | Phone | Pager app |
| Head of platform | Phone | Assistant's phone |

- A page not acknowledged on the primary within its own window **repeats on the fallback**.
- A page unacknowledged on **both** is treated as **unreachable**, and the sender **moves on** rather than waiting. In practice: unreachable at a rung means you climb, and you record it as unreachable.
- Channel changes take effect on the **next shift**, not immediately, so a directory change made mid-incident does not silently redirect a page already in flight. If someone tells you mid-incident that their number changed, keep paging the number the directory held when the page went out.

> **Where the material is silent:** the directory says a page repeats on the fallback "within its own window" but never states the length of that window for any role. You cannot compute it from the escalation clocks. Page the primary, and if you have no acknowledgement well before the rung's escalation clock expires, page the fallback rather than letting the rung clock run out on an unattempted fallback.

### 5.4 What every climb must write

Each climb writes a line to the incident record containing:

1. The rung it left.
2. The rung it reached.
3. The clock that expired.
4. Whether it expired **unacknowledged**.

Write this line at the moment of the climb, not retrospectively.

---

## 6. What is communicated while the incident is open

### 6.1 The opening notice

Send it as soon as the incident is opened. It contains three things and no more:

1. **What is affected** — e.g. the nightly reconciliation has not completed for the three named business dates; those dates' settled-invoice-to-ledger comparison is unproved.
2. **What is not affected** — state this explicitly. For a band B incident, the defining condition is that no external figure is yet affected; if that is true here, say so.
3. **When the next update will come.**

**The opening notice does not say what the cause is.** At that point nobody knows, and the guide's stated reason is that a guess in an opening notice outlives the incident.

> **Where the material is silent:** no default update cadence is specified for band B or for any band. The guide only requires that the opening notice *promise* a cadence and that updates then hold to it. Choose one, state it in the opening notice, and hold to it.

### 6.2 Updates

- Updates go out on **the cadence the opening notice promised**, including the ones that say nothing has changed. **A silent incident is read as a resolved one.**
- **Only the incident lead speaks to anyone outside the platform group.** The stated reason is not secrecy: two well-meaning people describing the same partial picture produce three versions of it. Route every external question — including from finance — through the lead.
- **Language to avoid:** "should be fixed", "briefly", "minor". Say what was observed and what was done.

> **Where the material is silent:** the communication guide relies on an "incident lead" but no available page defines who that is, how the role is assigned, or whether it is the opener, the first rung, or the duty manager. Name the lead explicitly in the incident record at open, so that the single-voice rule has someone to attach to, and flag the undefined role as a correction candidate in the postmortem (§10).

### 6.3 Finance and the close calendar

The reconciliation is a control over ledger data, so the close calendar governs what you may do while fixing it:

- A **close period** runs to the last working day of the month. **Records dated inside a closed period are never restated in place**; a correction is posted into the open period with a reference back. If any of the three unreconciled business dates fall inside a period that has since closed, that is an accounting matter, not a platform one — it goes to finance through the incident lead.
- Platform changes touching anything the ledger reads are **frozen from the last working day of the month to the second working day of the next**. **The freeze does not stop an incident response**, but a change applied during a freeze for incident reasons **must be recorded as such**. Check the calendar before you change anything; as of 2026-08-09 the date sits mid-month, outside that window, but verify rather than assume.

---

## 7. Diagnosis, in the order the material supports

Work these in order. Record each observation in the timeline as you make it, including observations that turn out to be irrelevant — the postmortem standard explicitly requires them.

### 7.1 Establish which input is missing

The job fails when it cannot read one of its two inputs, and this usually means the **ledger extract has not landed**. The extract is due nightly at 03:40 (by 06:00 on the first two working days of a month).

### 7.2 Check the manifest first

The extract arrives from the finance system as a single file with a manifest carrying a **row count and a checksum**. The extract is **not considered delivered until both match**. The manifest is the first thing to look at, because it splits the diagnosis in two:

| What you find | What it means | Where it goes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A manifest with no file | The **transfer failed** | Upstream, one contact |
| **No manifest at all** | The **upstream job did not run** | Upstream, a *different* contact |
| A file whose row count is **below** its manifest | **Truncated** — it is **quarantined, not loaded** | Do not load it manually |

The truncation rule matters even though the job is currently failing rather than loading: a truncated extract that *is* loaded looks exactly like a night on which finance posted very little, and the difference is only discovered a period later. Never work around a quarantine to get the job green.

> **Where the material is silent:** the delivery runbook states that the two missing-extract cases "go to different people" but does not name either contact, team, or channel. Identify them from the finance-system side before paging anyone upstream, and record in the incident which contact you used and how you found them — that gap is itself a correction candidate for §10.

### 7.3 Compare against the known failure patterns

Eleven failures in the last two years group into three causes. Use these as hypotheses, not conclusions:

- **Late extract** — by far the most common. The upstream file had not landed when the job started. **Every one of these cleared on the next schedule.** This pattern is therefore a poor fit for three consecutive nights.
- **Schema drift** — the extract gained a column and the loader rejected the file. Two occurrences, **both after an upstream release**. Ask whether the finance system released in the last three days.
- **Consecutive failures** — this has happened once before, on exactly three consecutive nights, caused by **a transfer credential that had expired** and was renewed only after the third morning. **That run is the reason the consecutive-failure case is now handled explicitly rather than as three unrelated single failures.** Given the shape of the current situation, check credential expiry early.

### 7.4 Check what ran downstream on partial input

This is the check the Overnight Failure Review names as the one that gets missed, because **a job that succeeded on incomplete input leaves no failure anywhere**. For each of the three nights, establish whether anything downstream of the reconciliation ran, and on what input. Record the answer even when it is "nothing did."

Also check whether the reconciliation window (04:00–05:30) was itself displaced. A job that overruns its window is not killed, but the window behind it starts late and the delay accumulates across the night. If an earlier window overran, the reconciliation may have been starting before its input was due.

---

## 8. Manual runs — what they settle and what they do not

Once the missing input has actually landed, the reconciliation can be run by hand for a named business date. Do this to settle the numbers; do not do it expecting to close the incident.

**Procedure:**
1. Run it from the platform host with the business date.
2. It takes **one business date and both of that date's inputs**. It **refuses to start if either input is absent** — the same refusal the scheduled run makes, and for the same reason: a reconciliation against one side is not a reconciliation. Do not try to defeat this refusal.
3. Wait for the break count.
4. **Read the breaks, not the exit code.**
5. **An enormous break count almost always means the extract was for a different date.** Treat that as a signal to stop and re-check the input, not as a real result.

**What it settles:** the numbers for that date.
**What it does not settle:** whether the scheduled job is healthy. It is **not** evidence that the next night will run, and **a manual run does not clear an open incident.**

**If the manual runs produce breaks,** those are worked separately through break triage, and their categories carry their own handling:
- **Timing** — the two sides saw the same event on different days; clears itself on the next run; only worth investigating when **the same key breaks on three separate nights**.
- **Sign** — same magnitude, opposite direction; almost always a refund recorded as a charge upstream; **does not self-clear**.
- **Orphan** — one side has a record the other has never seen. **An orphan older than one close period stops being a data question and becomes an accounting one**, and is handed to finance with the record rather than resolved in the platform.

---

## 9. What has to be true before the incident can be closed

Closing requires **evidence that the condition has gone, not an absence of further reports**.

For a scheduled job, that evidence is defined precisely: **a clean scheduled run.** Both the incident-mechanics page and the job runbook state it — the incident closes on the evidence that the *scheduled* run has recovered, not on a successful manual one.

**Closure checklist — all must be true:**

1. A **scheduled** run of `ledger-reconcile` has completed cleanly. Not a manual run, not a re-triggered ad-hoc run.
2. Every escalation climb, expiry, and late acknowledgement has been written into the record (§5.4).
3. The three unreconciled business dates have been settled by manual run, or the fact that they have not been, and why, is recorded and handed to finance through the lead.
4. The downstream check from §7.4 has an answer recorded for each of the three nights.
5. Any change applied during a ledger freeze has been recorded as an incident-reason freeze change (§6.3).
6. A closing communication has gone out on the promised cadence, in the observed-and-done language of §6.2.

**An incident is never deleted.** If this one turns out to have been opened by mistake — say the third failure was a break report misread as a failure — it is **closed as opened by mistake**, not removed. The record that somebody thought this was wrong is itself worth keeping.

> **Where the material is silent:** nothing specifies how many clean scheduled runs are needed. The stated requirement is "a clean scheduled run," singular. Given that the prior consecutive-failure episode ran three nights, note in the record if you choose to hold the incident open for a second clean night, and say why.

---

## 10. The record it has to leave behind

Every closed incident leaves a record, **whatever its band**. It has four parts, and all four are required.

**1. Timeline.** What was observed and when, in the order it was observed — **including the observations that turned out to be irrelevant**. This is why §7 asks you to write as you go. The escalation lines from §5.4 belong here.

**2. Contributing conditions.** The conditions that had to hold for the incident to happen, **written as conditions rather than as causes**, because the useful ones are usually the conditions nobody chose. For this incident, candidates visible from the material itself include: the extract being due 20 minutes before the reconciliation window opens; automatic retry masking single failures so that three nights is the first signal; the batch review shift carrying no pager; and, if credential expiry is the cause again, the absence of any expiry warning.

**3. Corrections.** What changed as a result, **each with an owner**. **A correction with no owner is a wish and is not recorded as a correction.** Carry the documentation gaps this document had to flag (§11) in here as correction candidates.

**4. Review.** The record is read by **someone who was not involved**. The reviewer's job is to find the part of the timeline that only makes sense to the people who were there.

> **Where the material is silent:** no deadline is specified for producing the record, and no process is given for selecting the reviewer beyond their not having been involved.

---

## 11. While the incident is open: handover

- The night shift handover is **written, not spoken, and written as the night goes** rather than at the end of it. It records which jobs completed, which failed and whether they were retried, anything left running deliberately, and anything the morning review should look at even though it did not fail.
- **An open incident is never handed over in the notes alone.** The outgoing engineer **speaks** to the incoming one, **and the notes record that they did.** The on-call handbook repeats this: an incident with an open clock is never handed over silently.
- Remember that escalation clocks **run across the handover**. Hand over the open timestamp and which rung the incident currently sits on, not just the symptom.

---

## 12. Consolidated list of gaps in the available material

Each of these should be raised as a correction with an owner in the postmortem (§10, part 3).

1. The **owning team** for `ledger-reconcile` is never named; the ladder refers only to "the owning team's shift lead."
2. The **amber route's third-rung 2-hour clock has no destination** — the route ends at the head of platform.
3. The **page acknowledgement window** ("within its own window") has no stated length for any role.
4. No **update cadence** is specified for band B; the guide only requires that the opening notice promise one.
5. The **incident lead** role is relied on by the communication guide but defined nowhere.
6. The **two upstream contacts** for a missing manifest versus a missing file are distinguished but not named.
7. No **incident tracking system** is named for opening the record.
8. No **deadline or reviewer-selection process** is given for the postmortem record.
9. It is unstated whether a **successful manual run breaks the consecutive-failure count**, and whether **one** clean scheduled run or more is required to close.

# order-refunds — Export Onboarding Document

**Status:** onboarding draft. `order-refunds` is a new nightly export to be operated exactly as `clickstream-raw` is operated. Everything below is drawn from the platform's recorded operating pages; where those pages are silent about `order-refunds` specifically, this document says so instead of filling the gap.

**Standing principle for this onboarding:** the pages that govern naming, zone layout, storage lifetime, landing time, and re-runs are written once for *every* export, and each of them keeps a central register (a table or a class list) that is the authority. Inheriting `clickstream-raw`'s behaviour is not the same as being registered — `order-refunds` must appear in those registers in its own right, because the purge and the run review read the register, not this document.

---

## 1. Naming

### 1.1 The convention

An export job is named `<subject>-<grain>`: lower case, hyphen separated, **no environment segment** — the environment is a property of the deployment, not of the job. (*Export Job Naming Convention*)

`order-refunds` is well formed against that shape: two lower-case segments, hyphen separated, no environment token. It parses as subject `order`, grain `refunds`.

**Gap:** the convention fixes the *shape* of the name but the recorded material does not publish a controlled vocabulary of valid `<grain>` tokens, and it gives no rule for whether `refunds` is a grain (as `raw` is in `clickstream-raw`) or a second subject qualifier. Nothing in the material blocks the name; if the platform group intends `<grain>` to be a grain-of-data token only, that reading should be confirmed with them before the name is fixed, because renaming afterwards is expensive (§1.3).

Note also that an export named `order-events` already exists in the delivery register. `order-refunds` and `order-events` share a subject segment; the recorded material does not treat that as a conflict, and each export gets its own prefix regardless (§2).

### 1.2 The output name

The output path repeats the job name. The output is therefore named `order-refunds` as well — there is no separate dataset name to choose, and no environment segment in the path name either. (*Export Job Naming Convention*)

### 1.3 Renaming later

If `order-refunds` is ever renamed, the rename is a **two-step change**:

1. Create the new name as an **alias** and write **both** names for one full window.
2. Retire the old name only once **no consumer has read it for a week**.

A rename that skips the alias step breaks every consumer that resolves the path by string rather than by catalog lookup — which in practice is most of them. (*Export Job Naming Convention*)

---

## 2. Where the output lands and how the area is organised

### 2.1 The raw zone

`order-refunds` lands in the **raw zone**, which holds:

- **one bucket per environment**, and
- **one prefix per export**.

Underneath the prefix, partitions are laid out by the export's **declared partition columns in declaration order**, so the same path shape works for every export in the zone. (*Raw Zone Layout*; *Export Job Naming Convention*)

So the path shape for this export is: *raw-zone bucket for the environment* → `order-refunds/` → *partition columns, in declaration order*.

**Gaps:**
- The recorded material does not name the raw-zone buckets for any environment. The bucket names must come from the platform group.
- **The partition columns for `order-refunds` are not declared anywhere in the recorded material.** This is the single most important open item in this document, because the path layout, the unit of re-run (§5), and the unit of purge (§3) are all defined in terms of partitions. `clickstream-raw` writes the previous day's data as **hourly partitions**, and every operating procedure that this export is meant to inherit — single-hour re-run, "the export is idempotent per partition", lateness measured at the last partition written — assumes an hourly grain. Operating `order-refunds` "exactly like `clickstream-raw`" implies the same business-date-plus-hour partitioning, but the material does not state it for this export, so it must be declared explicitly at onboarding rather than assumed from this document.

### 2.2 The rule against writing outside your own prefix

**Nothing writes outside its own prefix.** A job that needs to read another export's output reads it **in place**; copying it under a second prefix produces two datasets that drift apart and are both believed. (*Raw Zone Layout*)

Applied here, concretely:
- `order-refunds` writes only under the `order-refunds` prefix. It must not write into `order-events`, `clickstream-raw`, or any other export's prefix, even for a convenience copy.
- If `order-refunds` needs `order-events` (or any other export) as input, it reads it in place.
- Equally, no other job may write into the `order-refunds` prefix.

### 2.3 Finding the prefix

The zone is **not browsable by hand at any useful scale**. Consumers and operators resolve the prefix through the **catalog entry** for the export, not by listing the bucket — on the larger exports a listing takes minutes and returns tens of thousands of keys. (*Raw Zone Layout*)

**Gap:** a catalog search of this platform returns no catalog entity for `order-refunds` — and none for `clickstream-raw` either. The material states that consumers are expected to resolve prefixes via the catalog, so **creating the catalog entry for `order-refunds` is part of onboarding**, but the recorded material does not describe the mechanics of registering an export in the catalog (who does it, what fields it carries). That procedure has to come from the platform group.

### 2.4 File layout after writing (compaction)

A partition lands as **many small files, one per writer**. Compaction rewrites them into a few large ones once the file count crosses a trigger that is **set per dataset and defaults to two hundred files**. Compaction runs **opportunistically inside the maintenance window** (00:45–02:00, §4.1) and is **safe to skip** — a skipped partition is simply compacted the following night. (*Partition Compaction Notes*; *Nightly Batch Window Calendar*)

Compaction changes the layout and **nothing else**. In particular the partition keeps its **original write date**, because every lifecycle decision downstream is made against that original date; a compaction that reset the date would quietly extend the life of everything it touched. (*Partition Compaction Notes*) See §3.2 and §5.4.

At onboarding, either accept the 200-file default trigger for `order-refunds` or set a per-dataset value. The material gives no basis for choosing a non-default value here.

---

## 3. Storage registration and how long the output lives

### 3.1 The register

**Every dataset the platform writes is registered under one storage class.** The class fixes both the tier the bytes land on and the window after which they are purged. **Nothing else sets a lifetime** — a job that wants its output kept longer is asking to be reclassified, not asking for a change to the job. (*Storage Class Register*)

| Class | Tier | Purge window |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SC-1 | hot | 7 days |
| SC-2 | hot | 30 days |
| SC-3 | warm | 45 days |
| SC-4 | warm | 62 days |
| SC-5 | cold | 400 days |
| SC-6 | archive | held indefinitely |

### 3.2 What applies to order-refunds

`clickstream-raw` is registered under **storage class SC-4** — warm tier, **62-day purge window** — and the export itself sets no lifetime of its own. (*Clickstream Raw Export Runbook*)

Operated exactly like `clickstream-raw`, `order-refunds` is registered under **SC-4: warm tier, purged 62 days after write date.**

**This registration is an action, not an inheritance.** The register is a central list and the purge **reads the register, not the request** — a class is never changed or assumed in place for a single dataset without updating the register. `order-refunds` must be added to the Storage Class Register as SC-4 before it writes anything, or its retention behaviour is undefined by the platform's own rules. (*Storage Class Register*)

**How the purge behaves:** it runs **daily** and removes **whole objects** once their write date is older than the window. An object is **never partially removed**, so a window boundary falling inside an object keeps the whole object until the next boundary. Combined with §2.4: the write date used is the *original* write date, unchanged by compaction, and unchanged by a re-run (§5.4). (*Storage Class Register*; *Partition Compaction Notes*; *Export Re-run Procedure*)

**Consideration flagged, not decided:** SC-4 is the class that matches "operated exactly like `clickstream-raw`", and that is what this document specifies. Refund records may carry financial or regulatory retention expectations that a 62-day warm window does not satisfy. The recorded material contains no retention requirement for refund data and no rule mapping data subject to storage class, so this document does not assume one — but the owning team should confirm 62 days is acceptable *before* go-live, because changing it afterwards is a reclassification (§3.3) reviewed on a monthly cycle.

### 3.3 If the class ever needs to change

Reclassification requests are **reviewed monthly**. A move **up** the tiers (cold→warm, warm→hot) needs a **stated reason for the extra cost**; a move **down** needs **confirmation from the owning team that nothing reads the older partitions**. Either way the register itself is updated, because the purge reads the register. (*Storage Class Register*)

A request to keep a particular partition longer than the class allows is a reclassification request — it is **not** a change to the export job. (*Clickstream Raw Export Runbook*)

---

## 4. When it is expected to land, and repeated lateness

### 4.1 The overnight schedule

The night is divided into windows, each owned by one job family:

| Window | Owner |
| --- | --- |
| 22:00 – 23:15 | collector drain |
| 23:15 – 00:45 | **raw exports** |
| 00:45 – 02:00 | maintenance and vacuum |
| 02:00 – 04:00 | aggregation |
| 04:00 – 05:30 | reconciliation |

`order-refunds` is a raw export, so it runs in the **23:15 – 00:45** window. A job that overruns its window is **not killed**, but the window behind it starts late and **the delay accumulates across the night** — an overrunning `order-refunds` pushes maintenance, then aggregation, then reconciliation. (*Nightly Batch Window Calendar*)

Moving a window is a **scheduling change, not a job change**: the request goes to the platform group with the reason and the earliest night it can take effect. A move that pushes any window past 05:30 needs the **aggregation owner's agreement**, because the morning reports read what aggregation writes. (*Nightly Batch Window Calendar*)

### 4.2 The expected landing hour

Each nightly export has an **expected landing hour, measured at the moment its last partition is written** — not when the job starts. The registered expectations are:

| Export | Expected by |
| --- | --- |
| clickstream-raw | 02:00 |
| order-events | 02:30 |
| ledger-extract | 03:40 |

(*Export Delivery Expectations*)

**Gap and required action:** **the table has no row for `order-refunds`.** Operated exactly like `clickstream-raw`, its expected landing hour is **02:00**, and that is the value this document proposes. But the table is the authority the morning review measures against, so `order-refunds` must be **added to it explicitly** — an export absent from the table has no expectation to be late against. The proposed 02:00 should be sanity-checked against §4.1: the raw-export window closes at 00:45, so 02:00 leaves the same margin `clickstream-raw` has, but if `order-refunds` is materially slower or has a later upstream dependency, the registered hour should reflect that rather than being copied.

Note the delivery page states plainly: **nothing there says how long a delivered export is kept — landing and lifetime are separate concerns with separate owners.** Landing is §4; lifetime is §3.

### 4.3 What "late" means and what happens

- Lateness is counted in **whole hours past the expected time**.
- It is **reported in the morning run review**.
- **An export that is late three mornings in a row is raised with its owning team**, because at that point either the expectation is wrong or the job is. (*Export Delivery Expectations*)

The morning review is the mechanism that catches this. Every morning one engineer reviews the night's failures; the review is **a reading, not a repair** — anything needing a fix is handed to the owning team with what the review found. The review deliberately **reads three nights at a time rather than one**: a job that failed once is noise, and the same job failing on consecutive nights is the thing the review exists to notice, which is only visible to someone looking across nights. For each failure it hands on: the job, the nights involved, whether it recovered on its own, and **whether anything downstream ran on partial input** — the last being the one that gets missed, because a job that succeeded on incomplete input leaves no failure anywhere. (*Overnight Failure Review*)

For `order-refunds` this means the three-night rule and the three-night review window line up: the third consecutive late morning is both the trigger for raising it and the point at which the review is looking at the full pattern.

**A distinction that matters overnight:** a job **fails** when it cannot complete; a job **reports a problem** when it completes and does not like what it saw. These are worked by different people on different clocks, and conflating them is the reason most overnight pages reach the wrong person. A late-but-successful `order-refunds` drop is not a failure. (*Platform Glossary*) Similarly, a **missing drop** is a delivery that did not arrive; a **late drop** is one that arrived outside its window. (*Platform Glossary*)

### 4.4 Gaps around lateness

- **The owning team for `order-refunds` is not recorded anywhere in the available material.** "Raised with its owning team" and "the owning team's shift lead" both presuppose a named owner. A named, pageable owner must be recorded at onboarding. (The one onboarding checklist in the material that requires "name an owner who can be paged" is the *Stream Onboarding Checklist*, which covers putting a producer on a stream and explicitly does not cover exports — so it is a useful precedent, not an applicable procedure.)
- **The material does not connect repeated lateness to an escalation ladder or an incident.** *Export Delivery Expectations* says lateness is raised with the owning team; it does not say an incident is opened. The platform does maintain escalation routes — **Standard** (owning team's shift lead → owning team's manager, working hours only), **Amber** (shift lead → platform duty manager → head of platform), **Red** (shift lead → duty manager → head of platform → executive on call) — with clocks held separately (Standard: 4 hours on the first rung, then next working day; doubled between 22:00 and 06:00. Amber: 20 / 25 minutes / 2 hours. Red: 5 / 10 / 30 minutes; Red and Amber run the same clocks at every hour). But **nothing in the recorded material assigns a route or a severity band to a late export**, and this document does not invent one. If the owning team wants repeated lateness to page rather than merely be raised, that mapping has to be agreed and recorded separately. (*Escalation Ladders*; *Duty Manager Response Matrix*)

---

## 5. Re-running after a bad night

The re-run procedure is written once for every export and applies to `order-refunds` as written. (*Export Re-run Procedure*)

### 5.1 The governing property

**A re-run replaces what it writes.** Exports here are **idempotent per partition**, so re-running one hour rewrites that hour and leaves the rest of the night alone. This is what makes a re-run safe without a cleanup step. (*Export Re-run Procedure*; *Clickstream Raw Export Runbook*)

This depends on `order-refunds` actually being partitioned per hour and actually being idempotent per partition — see the gap in §2.1. Confirm both before relying on the single-hour path.

### 5.2 Single-hour re-run — the usual case

Used after an upstream source was late.

1. Re-run the single hour, **not the whole night**.
2. **Tell the downstream jobs that read it.**

Note the shape of that second step in the `clickstream-raw` case: the downstream sessionization job needs **a re-run of the whole business date, not of the hour**, because it is idempotent per business date and re-running it replaces that date's output entirely rather than appending. A late partition is handled by re-running the date once the partition has landed, **never** by patching the output. (*Export Re-run Procedure*; *Sessionization Job Runbook*)

**Gap:** the recorded material names **no downstream consumers of `order-refunds`**. Sessionization reads `clickstream-raw`, not this export. "Tell the downstream jobs that read it" cannot be executed until the consumers of `order-refunds` are identified and recorded, and the re-run grain each of them needs (hour vs. whole business date) is known. Establishing that consumer list is an onboarding prerequisite, not a later refinement — a single-hour re-run with an unnotified downstream is exactly the "downstream ran on partial input" case the morning review says gets missed (§4.3).

### 5.3 Whole-night re-run

Reserved for **one case only: the export ran against the wrong business date.**

- A whole-night re-run writes every hour again and **is safe**.
- **It does not remove the partitions written under the wrong date.** Those are **removed by hand**, and **until they are, both dates look complete.** (*Export Re-run Procedure*)

Treat the manual removal as part of the re-run, not as follow-up work. A wrong-date partition left in place under the `order-refunds` prefix is indistinguishable from a correct one to anything reading the zone.

### 5.4 What a re-run does not do

**A re-run never changes an object's original write date, so it does not extend anything's life in the raw zone.** (*Export Re-run Procedure*) A partition re-run on day 60 of its SC-4 window is still purged on schedule against its original write date (§3.2). If output must survive longer, that is a reclassification (§3.3), not a re-run.

### 5.5 A precedent worth borrowing, with a caveat

The `clickstream-raw` runbook's first diagnostic is that **a missing hourly partition is almost always an upstream source that has not drained rather than an export failure** — check upstream lag first, then re-run the single hour. Its upstream discipline is: restart a stuck collector rather than draining it by hand, because **a hand-drained collector writes a partial partition, and a partial partition is indistinguishable from a complete one once it has landed**; if a restart does not clear it, mark the hour as **held**, let the export run without it, and re-export the hour once the source is healthy. (*Clickstream Raw Export Runbook*; *Event Collector Drain Runbook*)

**Gap:** `clickstream-raw` waits for an explicit **drain signal** from the event collectors before it starts. **The recorded material does not say what `order-refunds` reads, whether it has an equivalent upstream gate, or what its "not yet ready" signal is.** The partial-partition hazard and the "mark the hour held, re-export later" pattern are general enough to be worth adopting, but the specific drain-signal and lag mechanics are collector-specific and cannot be assumed to exist for this export. Define `order-refunds`'s upstream readiness condition explicitly at onboarding.

---

## 6. If any output is ever copied outside the platform

### 6.1 What counts

**Any route that writes platform data to a destination the platform does not operate is an egress — whether it runs once or nightly.** A copy of `order-refunds` partitions to a partner bucket is an egress. (*Data Egress Approval Policy*; *Clickstream Raw Export Runbook*, which flags exactly this case for its own partitions)

### 6.2 What approval requires

An egress needs **all three** before it is approved:

1. A **named recipient**.
2. A **stated purpose**.
3. An **end date**.

Approval sits with the **data governance group**. (*Data Egress Approval Policy*)

### 6.3 End dates are enforced, not reviewed

- **A route without an end date is not approved.**
- **A route whose end date has passed is disabled automatically rather than reviewed**, and **re-enabling it is a new request** — not an extension of the old one. (*Data Egress Approval Policy*)

Anyone depending on an `order-refunds` egress should track its end date as a hard cut-off; the route stops on that date without a conversation.

### 6.4 Per-run recording

**Every approved route records, per run, what it sent and how much of it.** The record is the point of the approval: an egress nobody can describe afterwards is **indistinguishable from one that was never approved**. (*Data Egress Approval Policy*)

An `order-refunds` egress must therefore emit a per-run record of content and volume from its first run, not once someone asks.

### 6.5 Current position

**No egress route for `order-refunds` exists in the recorded material, approved or proposed.** Until one is approved by the data governance group under §6.2, `order-refunds` output stays inside the platform boundary. Nothing in this document authorises a copy out; it states the conditions any future copy would have to meet.

Note also that the recorded material contains **no data classification for refund data** — no tag, glossary term, or sensitivity marking for `order-refunds` was found. Refund records commonly carry customer and payment detail. The egress policy above is the only recorded control that would apply, and it is a process control, not a content control. If refund data warrants a classification or access restriction, that determination has to be made by the data governance group; this document cannot ground one.

---

## 7. Onboarding checklist

Actions that must complete before `order-refunds` runs in production. Items marked **[gap]** are not answerable from the recorded material and need a decision from the named group.

| # | Action | Authority / source |
| --- | --- | --- |

| 2 | **Declare the partition columns, in declaration order** (hourly, matching `clickstream-raw`, unless decided otherwise) **[gap]** | owning team / *Raw Zone Layout* |
| 3 | Create the `order-refunds` prefix in the raw-zone bucket for each environment **[gap: bucket names not recorded]** | platform group / *Raw Zone Layout* |
| 4 | Create the **catalog entry** so consumers resolve the prefix by lookup, not by bucket listing **[gap: registration mechanics not recorded]** | platform group / *Raw Zone Layout* |
| 5 | **Register `order-refunds` in the Storage Class Register as SC-4** (warm, 62 days) | *Storage Class Register* |
| 6 | Confirm 62 days meets any refund-data retention expectation **[gap: none recorded]** | owning team + data governance group |
| 7 | Set or accept the compaction trigger (default 200 files) | *Partition Compaction Notes* |
| 8 | **Add `order-refunds` to the Export Delivery Expectations table** with an expected landing hour (proposed: **02:00**) | *Export Delivery Expectations* |
| 9 | Confirm the job fits the **23:15–00:45 raw-export window** and will not overrun it | *Nightly Batch Window Calendar* |
| 10 | **Record a named, pageable owning team** **[gap]** | *Export Delivery Expectations*; *Escalation Ladders* |
